content: Marfan syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene, which affects connective tissue throughout the body. This condition impacts multiple organ systems, including the cardiovascular, ocular, skeletal, dural, and pulmonary systems. Among these, the cardiovascular system is most notably affected, with aortic root dilatation being the most common manifestation. Complications of aortic root dilatation, such as aortic regurgitation, dissection, and rupture, are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in individuals with Marfan syndrome. The objective of this study was to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of beta-blocker therapy compared to placebo, no treatment, or surveillance in individuals with Marfan syndrome. A systematic search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, was conducted on June 28, 2017. Additional searches were performed in resources such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were placed on the language of publication. The inclusion criteria required randomized controlled trials (RCTs) lasting at least one year, involving participants of any age with a confirmed diagnosis of Marfan syndrome, and comparing beta-blocker monotherapy to placebo, no treatment, or surveillance. One open-label, single-center RCT met the inclusion criteria. This study included 70 participants with Marfan syndrome, aged 12 to 50 years, who were randomly assigned to either propranolol treatment (32 participants) or no treatment (38 participants). The average duration of follow-up was 9.3 years in the control group and 10.7 years in the treatment group. Propranolol was initiated at a dose of 10 mg four times daily, with the dose titrated to achieve a heart rate below 100 beats per minute during exercise or a 30% increase in the systolic time interval. The mean optimal dose of propranolol was 212 ± 68 mg per day, divided into four doses. The study found that beta-blocker therapy did not reduce the incidence of all-cause mortality (relative risk [RR] 0.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.01 to 4.75; 70 participants; low-quality evidence). Mortality specifically attributed to Marfan syndrome was not reported. Non-fatal serious adverse events were also not reported. However, the study did assess pre-defined non-fatal clinical endpoints, including aortic dissection, aortic regurgitation, cardiovascular surgery, and congestive heart failure. No significant differences were observed between the treatment and control groups for these outcomes (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.69; 70 participants; low-quality evidence). Specifically, beta-blocker therapy did not significantly reduce the incidence of aortic dissection (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.12 to 3.03), aortic regurgitation (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.18 to 7.96), congestive heart failure (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.18 to 7.96), or cardiovascular surgery (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.12 to 3.03; 70 participants; low-quality evidence). However, the study reported a reduced rate of aortic dilatation in the treatment group, as measured by M-mode echocardiography (aortic ratio mean slope: 0.084 in the control group vs. 0.023 in the treatment group; P < 0.001). Changes in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, total adverse events, and withdrawal due to adverse events were not reported for either group at the study's endpoint. The study was judged to have a high risk of bias in several domains, including selection bias (allocation concealment), performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, and selective reporting bias. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low. It remains unclear whether the observed reduction in the rate of aortic dilatation translates into meaningful clinical benefits, such as reduced rates of aortic dissection or mortality. In conclusion, based on the findings of this single, low-quality RCT, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the clinical efficacy of long-term propranolol therapy in individuals with Marfan syndrome. High-quality randomized trials are needed to assess the long-term benefits and risks of beta-blocker therapy in this population. Future studies should report on all clinically relevant endpoints and adverse events to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the therapy's benefit-risk profile.
